title: Crosses of many lands

segments.voice: Yesterday, churches around the world: a round church in a ring of trees, red crosses over a city at night. Your line was many shapes. Which building did you look at twice? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-eight.

On the inside of a wrist, just below the palm, a small blue cross, inked into the skin. It doesn't wash off. Some Coptic Christians in Egypt wear one for life. Now lay other crosses beside it. A gray stone cross in an Irish field, taller than a man, with a ring around its center. A silver cross from Ethiopia, held in a priest's hand, its arms opening out into patterns like lace. A cross from a Russian church with three bars, the lowest one slanting. Four lands, four shapes, and every one of them points to the same cross. Today: crosses of many lands.
screen: `A RING, A LACE, A SLANTED BAR.`

segments.voice: Start in Ireland and Scotland, with the Celtic cross: a ring set around the place where the arms meet. What did the ring first mean? Some see a halo, some the sun, some a circle with no end. Others think it simply helped hold the stone arms up. The stone doesn't explain itself. Next, Egypt. Some Coptic Christians carry a small cross tattooed on the inner wrist, some from childhood. It's a way of belonging that can't be taken off. Paul once wrote to the Galatians, "I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus." Many readers take him to mean his scars. A wrist cross is a gentler mark, but it's worn in the same spirit: the body itself carries the sign. Then Ethiopia. Priests there may carry a hand cross of metal or wood, its arms opening into woven patterns, and people come up to kiss it and be blessed. The styles differ from place to place and from maker to maker. Last, the Russian Orthodox cross, with three bars. The top bar stands for Pilate's sign. John says: "And Pilate wrote a title, and put it on the cross. And the writing was, JESUS OF NAZARETH THE KING OF THE JEWS." When the chief priests asked him to change it, Pilate said: "What I have written I have written." The slanted bottom bar is a footrest, and Orthodox tradition gives it a meaning too: it tilts up toward the thief who asked to be remembered. So many crosses, carved, inked, cast and painted. And underneath them all, one line from Jesus in Luke: "If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me."

Here's the practice: draw a cross from another tradition. Find a pen and paper. Settle, and breathe. Choose one: the Celtic cross with its ring, the Orthodox cross with three bars and a slanted foot, or an Ethiopian cross with patterned arms. Draw it plainly, and give its one special detail your care: the ring, the slanted foot, or the pattern in the arms. As you draw, think of the people who carry that shape: in a field, on a wrist, in a priest's hand. If you pray, you can pray for them as you draw. If you don't, let the drawing be a way of paying attention to strangers. The bell holds the time.
Crosses of many lands. Ringed, inked, woven, three-barred: one cross, shaped by the places that carry it.
Your line: many crosses. Today, if you see a cross anywhere, ask where its shape came from, and who first carved, cast or drew it that way. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Christians in different lands carry the cross in their own forms: Celtic high crosses with a ring, small crosses tattooed on the wrist by some Coptic Christians, Ethiopian hand crosses carried by priests to bless people, and three-barred crosses in Russian and other Orthodox churches.

notes: Audit: 'He meant his scars' (Galatians 6:17) softened to 'many readers take him to mean', since Paul doesn't say what the marks are.

Editor pass: 'Pilate nailed' changed to Pilate's sign as John has it; 'nobody knows for sure', 'often from childhood', 'priests often carry' and the Meskel 'every year' softened under the claims rule; the drawing practice reworded so it doesn't repeat day 1363's slow-line drawing.

Coptic wrist-cross tattoo: described as worn by 'some Coptic Christians', 'often from childhood'. Confirm with a Coptic Keeper; the link to Galatians 6:17 is the lesson's juxtaposition, not a claim that Copts cite it.
Celtic cross ring: the lesson says nobody knows for sure what it first meant and lists halo, sun, eternity and structural support as possibilities. Confirm.
Ethiopian hand crosses: 'priests there often carry a hand cross... and people come up to kiss it and be blessed'. Confirm.

Russian Orthodox three-bar cross: top bar as Pilate's title; slanted footrest tilted up toward the repentant thief (Luke 23:39–43) is attributed to Orthodox tradition. Confirm the direction and the tradition's wording.
Hook: 'a gray stone cross in an Irish field, taller than a man' is illustrative.
Original: መስቀል (Meskel), Ge'ez/Amharic for cross; the annual Meskel feast. Confirm spelling and pronunciation.
